extracted.intended_audience: general public; comedians and performers interested in managing controversy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for stand-up comedians on how to respond to public backlash: when and whether to write about the controversy, how to frame it onstage, and how to remain authentic without letting controversy define your material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let controversy become your content
rubrics_metrics.description: "Your content may have become controversy, but controversy will never become your content."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Das's rule: even if a piece of content sparks controversy, avoid making that controversy the central subject matter of your new material. Instead of rehashing or centering the original contested content, refer briefly to the event and move on to other comedic territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address controversy by focusing on aftermath and self-reflection, not defense
rubrics_metrics.description: When mentioning the controversy, do not defend the original material or re-present it; describe what happened afterward and use self-deprecation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from Das: he doesn't reference the content or defend it — he says a video went up, recounts what happened immediately after, explains how he mishandled it, and finds the comedy in his own mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pause before creating new material after backlash
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow time to process before writing jokes about a controversy; Das waited "at least two months or three months" before writing his first joke after the incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This timing is presented as a deliberate rule to avoid reactive, rushed, or tone-deaf material and to give the performer space to reflect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid painting yourself as victim or hero
rubrics_metrics.description: "The tough thing is to never paint yourself as a victim or a hero."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for balanced perspective in storytelling — neither self-pity nor grandstanding. Present events honestly without elevating yourself to martyr or savior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't get stuck in a feedback loop reacting to previous work
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians can fall into a cycle of making new material that only reacts to their last special or controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break the loop by creating material that stands on its own rather than constantly responding to past controversies; this keeps comedy fresh and prevents career-defining reactive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and consider audience feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat feedback and differing opinions as valid; Das says any feedback or piece of evidence is a valid opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt humility: listen to criticism, avoid immediately assigning blame to others, and use feedback constructively when shaping responses or new material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize honesty and reveal personal identity onstage
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal of performing is that the audience should know who you are — your identity, country, and what you represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be candid and let personal identity inform your work; with age and experience, honesty in material tends to surface more quickly and helps audiences connect with the performer.
